The rules are very short, and a typical game lasts 30-45 minutes. But allow more time because you will want to play again and again! Each player gets an identical set of 28 tiles; then plays one per turn, trying to get their tiles in one unified group, while disrupting the tile groups of opposing players - capturing them only if unavoidable. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Playing the Game 2.1 Capturing 3 Game End 4 Two player game 5 BGA Scoring 6 Variants 6.1 Blockers Objective The goal of Uptown is to place your colored tiles in such a way that at the end of the game, they're connected in as few groups of as possible. A group is a collection of tiles of the same color which are all touching at least one other member of the group on at least one side (not just on a corner). Note: The number of groups is important, not the size of the groups. If two or more players have the same number of groups at the end of the game, the player who has captured the fewest of their opponents' tiles wins. See below for more about capturing. Playing the Game Below the board you can see the five tiles that are in your rack and available to place. On your turn, click one of these tiles, then click the space on the board where you want to place it. To be a legal move, the tile you're playing must match the board space where you're trying to place it. You can only place tiles with a letter on them (A-I) in the row with a matching label. You can only place tiles with a number (1-9) in the matching column. You can only place tiles with a symbol (man, ring, woman, street sign, skyline, saxophone, automobile, playing cards, champagne) in the area of the board with matching symbols on it. The dollar sign ($) tile is wild and you can place it anywhere. Your supply includes one tile of each letter, number, and symbol as well as a single dollar sign ($) tile. The game ends when each player has DRAWN (not played) all of their tiles and each player has taken a final turn (each player will have four un-played tiles). You can see how many tiles are left for you and your opponents to draw by looking at the number in the user information area in the top right corner of the page. Capturing If you wish to place a tile on a square where an opponent has already placed one of their tiles, you may do so. However, you may not split an opponent's tiles into more groups than they already had. You may also never capture one of your own tiles. You can see any tiles that your opponents have captured displayed below their names. Tiles that you have captured appear below your rack of tiles - a captured tile cannot be played. At the end of the game, if two or more players have the same number of groups, the player with fewest captured tiles wins. Game End After all players draw their final tiles, everyone gets one final turn and then the game ends. At the end of the game, you will have four un-played tiles left. Two player game Each player has two colors of tile, which are counted as separate colors for scoring (eg. a red tile next to a brown tile counts as two groups, even if they are owned by the same player). You can't capture your own other color. When you play a tile, draw one of the same color. If there are none left to draw, that color is now finished: set your four tiles of that color aside, and for the rest of the game you can only play the other color. When both players have finished their second color, the game ends. BGA Scoring BGA counts each distinct set of 1 or more tiles as 1 negative point, the closer your score is to 0 (and the fewer captures you've made) the better you are doing! If 2 or more players have the same score, the player with the fewest captures wins. [Rating: 1/10] There is winning strategy - place all of your tiles on the edges of the board and you won`t lose until somebody will do everything to destroy you.

[Rating: 1/10] Abstract and as dry as three million year-old bones. What a relief when it was over.

[Rating: 1/10] Tile placement, not my type. Simple and quick it seems, but no reason to play or play again.

[Rating: 2/10] Lack of Control. Others players didn't understand how to play and causes the game to break.

[Rating: 2/10] Though the game masquerades as a strategy game unfortunately it is too heavily influenced by luck. The strategy that does exist is trivial, assessing the best spot for a tile is incredibly easy. A wasted 20 minutes.

[Rating: 3/10] i found this quite playable but thoroughly disappointing.  not a whole lot going on.  don't like the rule about not being able to target players the way you might want, but the game might completely break down if that were allowed.  maybe there could be some safer middle ground regarding protected pieces, but i still don't see myself wanting to play the game.  toward the end it's clear who has a shot and who doesn't, but everyone has to keep on playing anyway.

[Rating: 3/10] An "okay" game. It probably plays better with more than 2 players though. Pretty competent, and it's easy to screw yourself up while not paying attention.

[Rating: 3/10] The beginning was a little interesting trying to place the tiles that will connect, Acquire style, but then I realized I am going to draw my entire set of tiles, so it's more about hoping others take your tiles.  Either way, scores will be very close and it really overstays its welcome - very tedious to play.

[Rating: 4/10] Seems like your goal would be to have the biggest blob.  Not true.  Your goal is to have the fewest number of blobs.  Size doesn't matter.  The game is a hybrid of Sudoku and a tile-laying game.  Alternatively, it's just like Acquire without the economics.  There just isn't much to get excited about.

[Rating: 4/10] Concept has potential, but really dislike the font and cheap clip art look of the board and pieces.

[Rating: 4/10] A very clever mechanism: 4 ways to reach a place (letter, number, symbol or $) with an almost perfect information on what is coming and what was used by the opponents. The rule not to separate a group of the same color gives all the spice (and the dynamic of space expansion).  Too bad, it has lot of qualities but is really really not my taste. Didn't manage to get any fun in this abstract game.
